With `dotnet new wpf` I can specify either `net6.0`, `net5.0`, `netcoreapp3.0` or `netcoreapp3.1`. The odd thing though is that if you specify `net6.0` you actually get `net6.0-windows`.
However I wanted to specify a TFM a bit more specific than the default, so I used `net6.0-windows10.0.19041.0`, which is a valid TFM for the WPF template, however I'm met with the following:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1378165/164758645-b8ae860a-500c-40fd-ae9d-1af92b281855.png)

Could the `-f` parameter be a little smarter and allow me to be more specific than the allowed TFMs, as long as it is a subset of them?

comments.body:
This is very closely related to https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/4159.

The core issue that prevents a quick and easy solution is that the TFM is used not only in template generation (what we call 'instantiation') but also in template selection.  Templates are grouped by a (GroupIdentity, TFM) tuple, because historically we've changed template _contents_ based on the TFM. Adding the ability to specify the newer, platform-specific TFMs would require us to make changes to the template selection code to do a kind of 'template TFM supports user TFM' check. This is a fairly invasive change that will require a lot of testing.

We've seen a number of issues popping up related to TFMs and how they interact with template selection and instantiation that lead to a poor user experience. Our current plan is to solve them at the root by disentangling TFMs from the generation process with a new template generator geared for .NET projects specifically, instead of the very generic generator we're currently using. That work is tracked by [this epic](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3208).  In the interim, the workaround I can suggest is to generate the project and change the TFM after the project is generated.

Extracted from https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/233

Create an item template for a dockerfile (for .NET projects)

This is currently blocked by https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3107 and https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3829 as there is no way to get information about the project such the output path of a project, its TFM, etc in order to correctly generate a dockerfile.

comments.body:
Spec:

* two images:
  * build image of `dotnet/sdk`, with an SDK docker image tag chosen based on the SDK version at the time of running the `dotnet new` command
  * runtime image, with the appropriate runtime base image (dotnet/runtime or dotnet/aspnet, based on the type of project) and runtime tag (based on the runtime version at time of running the `dotnet new` command)

Required inputs (may be derived from runtime execution at time of `dotnet new`, or specified explicitly during the `dotnet new` command as options):
* SDK version
  * Compute SDK_MAJOR_MINOR from this
* Runtime version (RUNTIME_IMAGE_TAG)
* Project output assembly name (PROJECT_OUTPUT_ASSEMBLY_NAME)
* Path to project file (PROJECT_FILE)
* All contents of project file (ALL_PROJECT_CONTENT)

Proposed Dockerfile template contents:
```dockerfile
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:<SDK_MAJOR_MINOR> AS build-env
WORKDIR /app

# Copy project file and restore as distinct layers
COPY <PROJECT_FILE> ./
RUN dotnet restore

# Copy everything else and build
COPY <ALL_PROJECT_CONTENT> ./
# publish RID-specific since we know the hosting OS/Architecture
RUN dotnet publish -c Release -o out --os linux --arch x64

# Build runtime image
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/<RUNTIME_IMAGE_NAME>:<RUNTIME_IMAGE_TAG>
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build-env /app/out .
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", <PROJECT_OUTPUT_ASSEMBLY_NAME>]
```

There's some overlap here with the proposed SDK User Story around [generating OCI Container Images from a project natively](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/issues/24216). If that progresses the need for this template item may be lessened.

I'd suggest using a non-root user by default together with a port > 1024 (e.g. 8080) to make sure that:
* The `Dockerfile` doesn't trigger repo scanning tools for misconfiguration warnings
* Running the container in Kubernetes won't be a problem even in presence of stricter configurations since requiring to run as non-root user is likely to become a common default with Pod Security Admission controller setups (PodSecurityPolicy on clusters compliant with CIS Benchmarks already require this and depending the underlying software, binding to a port < 1024 won't work as non-root user)

comments.body: @jianyexi can you give more info what you mean by scan? Is this during install or when instantiating template?
I mean it will open/stat the file during instantiating template
@vlada-shubina  & @JanKrivanek this will show up in the "to be triaged" list, as David was removed as assignee.

There are multiple reasons why processing of a folder with large number of files to skip is taking notrivial processing and in short the best advice is to avoid such a scenario. There are 3 main classes of issues leading to slow processing of tomplates with large amount of files to be skipped. We should fix the first one - this can bring up to 3 folds speedup (more realisticaly it'll half the time). Other 2 might need some prioritisation. Main classes of reasons why processing takes time: **1) Physically accessing the files that should be skipped.** This is a bug and should be fixed. Fixing should be quite easy. Each file is beeing opened and checked 4 times: This is caused by enumeration of file system entries within [`FileRenameGenerator.AugmentFileRenames`](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Orchestrator.RunnableProjects/FileRenameGenerator.cs#L45) which under the hood checks if the entry is a directory ([here](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Utils/PhysicalFileSystem.cs#L21)) - that call needs to open the file. The check for directory is called twice for each file entry (within the neumeration itself and then when wrapping into `FileSystemInfo`), and the whole `AugmentFileRenames` is called twice - once just to emulate changes and second time to perform the changes. Hence the 4 calls to open each file (including those that should be skipped). **How to fix:** Enumeration in `FileRenameGenerator` should perform a filtering (similar as e.g. in [`Orchestrator`](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Core/Util/Orchestrator.cs#L157)) and only entries of interest should be wrapped into custom objects (avoiding the need to check if entry is a directory) **2) Need to evaluate exclusion criteria for each entry.** Templating engine allows rich exclusion/inclusion semantic that leads to a nead to evaluate each single file/directory against the filters to determine whether it should or should not be processed: This logic can be seen e.g. in [`Orchestrator`](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Core/Util/Orchestrator.cs#L157) Only filenames are being checked - files are not being accessed. But still thousands of records can slow down processing. **How to fix:** Skipping of groups of files would require more complicated and involved logic in enumerating (that would traverse the file system recursively while for each directory deciding whether it should be skipped alltogether or visited) **3) Duplicated processing due to separated changes emulation and actual changes performing.** Template engine has 2 steps processing where in first step ([`RunnableProjectGenerator.GetCreationEffectsAsync`](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Orchestrator.RunnableProjects/RunnableProjectGenerator.cs#L100)) it performs all of the processing, but just records the results in memory - in order to determine possible destructive changes. If no destructive changes are detected (or if they are allowed with `--force` flag) then all processing is performed again ([`RunnableProjectGenerator.CreateAsync`](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Orchestrator.RunnableProjects/RunnableProjectGenerator.cs#L62)) and now written to destination. **How to fix:** This leads to many duplicated efforts (reading from filesystem; running macros; etc.). There are more effective techniques of performing rollback-enabled filesystem changes (e.g. performing the changes in temporary location first and then copying over to the requested destination). This would however require major changes in template engine processing. **Performance impact of the 3 categories:** Based on naive testing with repro case taking ~180 seconds to complete (couple thousands of files, while only 3 are to be processed): 1) _Renaming processing_ (`AugmentFileRenames`) - takes ~61.7% time 2) _Filtering of files to process_ (`GetFileChangesInternal` and `RunInteranl`) - takes ~36% time 3) _Double processing_ - each of those functions are executed twice, each execution taking similar amount of time.

We estimated only 1. item from above. 

After discussion, it seems that this issue appears only during template authoring. The template package should not include files to be excluded, therefore it unfortunately doesn't meet the bar to be addressed in .NET 7. 

Please comment if you feel blocked by this issue.

comments.body: Likely this is same as https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/4192. I need to dive deeper to see if underlying issue is already fixed.

Some deeper review notes:

Currently the design is to collect all of the options for each template in the template group (aka same GroupIdentity and generally same short name) into one set of completions. This is done by

* making a TemplateCommand for each template in the group
* parsing the context.CommandLineText with that command
* getting completions at the invoked cursor position for that parse result

A potential fix could be to check the parse errors at each iteration of the templates and not return results for templates that have parse errors.

I was stuck in https://github.com/dotnet/command-line-api/issues/1696 while trying implementing solution above. Parse errors occur even when the input is correct but not complete, and it doesn't allow to evaluate if input is valid for certain `TemplateCommand` at the moment. On the other hand, completions are returned even when input is wrong.
This needs further investigation.

body:
Right now there's no easy way to create a new .csproj targeting a different framework.

Add a way to specify which target framework(s) to use for the newly created project.

comments.body: @KirillOsenkov @KathleenDollard correct me if I'm wrong but I believe the `--framework` option allows you to do this. Transferring to the template engine, who owns dotnet new.

`--framework` has restricted list of values ( .NET Core\.NET tfms) . Targeting .NET framework is not intended.  

For some templates, including console, it is possible to override target framework using `--target-framework-override` option, however there is no validation. It just creates the same template having the value of `--target-framework-override` passed as `TargetFramework` in csproj. This feature is hidden. https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3261 

Tagging @baronfel to discuss support of .NET Framework TFMs in .NET SDK.

Note that I'm looking for a low-friction solution here. While `--target-framework-override` is nice and I didn't know about it, it has discoverability issues, and is plainly long to type. Remember, the goal of dotnet new is to simplify new project creation. If it is easier to just type up the .csproj by hand or edit the .csproj manually, dotnet new has lost its purpose as a utility to save users time.

We should definitely add `net472` and other desktop tfms to the --framework option, as well as see whether we can introduce a shorter shortcut such as `-f`, again, to save users some typing.

Thanks!
`-f` is already available as alias for `--framework`. We are also working on getting tab completion work now, including template options.

Nothing groundbreakingly new here, but here's where I see this issue currently:

There's a bit of a hurdle we've got to overcome here:
* SDKs no longer include _every_ TFM for different templates, so knowing the full set of TFMs that we have a particular template for is harder,
* the engine itself only advertises TFMs that it has templates for for completions,
* the engine itself uses the --framework parameter as a pivot to determine _which_ template to choose (see point 1), not as the TFM MSBuild property

Untangling these will be difficult, but to me the primary problem from a UX perspective is the overloaded use/meaning of the parameter.

We're tentatively looking at solving the TFM mismatches by a new template generator specifically for .NET projects, instead of the generic default generator. This will be tracked in [this epic](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3208).

body:
At the moment 2 cases for ambiguity may happen during template instantiation:
- different template groups may have same short name
- different templates in one group may have same precedence and it is not possible to determine the one to be run

Those cases may be solved by uninstalling one of the packages in template groups are coming from different packages, however if they are coming from single one the situation cannot be resolved.

Suggesting the following options to resolve these conflicts:
- `--group` allows to specify group identity to run
- `--identity` allows to specify template identity to run 


The error cases should be modified as following:
(ambiguous group)
`Unable to resolve the template, these templates matched your input:`
| Name | Short name | Group |
|---|---|---|
| Template 1 | short | Group.Identity1 |
| Template 2 | short | Group.Identity2 |         

`To run specific template, specify its group using --group option.`
`   dotnet new short --group Group.Identity1.`         

(ambiguous template)
`Unable to resolve the template, these templates matched your input:`
| Name | Short name | Identity |
|---|---|---|
| Template 1 | short | Templ.Identity1 |
| Template 2 | short | Templ.Identity2 |         

`This may happen due to authoring error or ambiguous parameter set`.
`To run specific template, specify the identity using --identity option.`
`    dotnet new short --identity Templ.Identity1 `

comments.body:
I like how explicit `-group` and `-identity` options are. At the same time, I think this may result in too much typing.

For instance, to instantiate editorconfig template from Boxed.Templates, one would need to type:
`dotnet new editorconfig --identity Dotnet.Boxed.editorconfig.CSharp`
which is much longer compared to
`dotnet new editorconfig`

The same happens with `--group` option.

---------------------
Maybe as an alternative, we can add a postfix to conflicting short names. For instance, if you have two templates with short name `editorconfig`, one could be renamed to `editorconfig2`. Numbers could be added according to the alphanumeric ordering of template package identifiers. If you delete/update template packages, the ordering and hence the short names may change.

Another option would be to support the template identity as the main parameter to `dotnet new`, in addition to the template short name.  This would allow for a greater degree of specificity and not have the duplication inherent in the `dotnet new <template short name> --identity <template identity>` example. One downside here is that the template identity may not be unique enough, or in some cases may be the same as the short name, so better tools for template authors to detect and fix these scenarios might be required.

> One downside here is that the template identity may not be unique enough, or in some cases may be the same as the short name, so better tools for template authors to detect and fix these scenarios might be required.

Template authors shouldn't be doing this. Instead of working around it, let's error when a user tries to install a template with a conflict on `identity`.
I can run my template analyzer to see if there are any duplicate IDs being used. I'll try to do that soon. I'm currently in the middle of some changes so I may need to wrap that up before hand.

Here is a JSON file (renamed as .txt to support GH) with all the templates that I could find. Will look for dupes later.
[template-report.json.txt](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/files/7590854/template-report.json.txt)

I ran my tool to identify templates that re-use the `identity` value across templates.

I only found 4 IDs that are actually being used in different templates.

There are three sides to this:
* Authoring
  * We should add validation to the templating build tasks that we already have - when `Pack`ing a template, we could check against the search json for duplicate `identity`ies to help the user not upload garbage data. Probably default this to not run when `Deterministic` is `true`, because we don't want to do network I/O on reproducible builds
* Installing
  * We should error when installing a template with an identity conflict (as such a template would be unusable). This should be overridable by the user via a `--force` flag similar to our other overrides on installation (e.g. the updated package templates override we added recently)
* Cleanup
  * We should reach out to the template owners that @sayedihashimi has noted above and work with them to deduplicate their identities ahead of any changes to the user experience here
For the `Authoring` case, I think this should be a warning and not an error.

body:
## Summary of issue

The `dotnet new gitignore` command saves a workflow step when scaffolding projects and really happy to see `dotnet new --install Microsoft.DotNet.Common.ItemTemplates::6.0.100` and those workflow improvements.  

Drift between gitignore templates or subtractions in the templates might introduce some security issues if secrets are checked in incorrectly for a new project or while doing a project refresh.  

As an example, patches from issues updated in a Feb, 2021 template here are not in a June, 2021 template on GitHub. 

## Repro

This is the first template which comes up in search results for Visual Studio gitignore when scaffolding a new project.  
https://github.com/github/gitignore/blob/master/VisualStudio.gitignore

It is different than the template generated using `dotnet new gitignore` from the `6.0.100` cli.
https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/template_feed/Microsoft.DotNet.Common.ItemTemplates/content/Gitignore/.gitignore

- The template here is missing nuget.config comment placeholder.  There's specific scenarios where nuget.config should or shouldn't be committed in 2021 and a comment indicating so rather than just removing nuget.config could be shown.  See https://github.com/NuGet/Home/issues/10566 and https://github.com/github/gitignore/pull/3706 - I don't know if this situation is resolved but it's impacting in terms of public/private feed credentials.  Also don't know if it's responsibility of this repo's maintainers to maintain the other repo's gitignore.
- The templating currently excludes .tye files here but not in Github.  Would be nice to have a unique identifier (not a url) and some more description about what .tye files are in the .gitignore to look up more info on what tye is and why someone would be ignoring the files from a binary, transitory or security perspective.  In any case these should be in synch.

## Suggestions

- Suggest some background task to synch this repo from GitHub gitignore, as two repos code / PRs diverge and improvements happen.  
- Source the template from github directly, with some option to download / refresh it for offline consumers.

- The template currently provided with dotnet new includes some additional exclusions for mac settings and things that are not really mac settings. Add these to the Github template if required, though are they really needed or is the workflow of a unique developer that could be added to personal/global gitignore?  When I see common .gitignore entries for mac, the gitignore list is a lot smaller and usually just include .DS_Store and thumbnails.  and config.make, tarballs, etc.

- The mac ignores look a little broad (eg. *.tar.gz is not mac-specific, it's a binary archive format) and what is "Mac bundle stuff".  The comments could be more specific and professional if introduced via this repo's contributions.  These will be in every dotnet project.

As a templating library, could enforce further rules and guidance for .gitignore comments, security and ensure standardization in the gitignore for dotnet.

----
Files to sync:

|File|Source|Target|
|---|---|---|
|`.gitignore`| [github/gitignore](https://github.com/github/gitignore/blob/master/VisualStudio.gitignore)| [dotnet/sdk](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/main/template_feed/Microsoft.DotNet.Common.ItemTemplates/content/Gitignore/.gitignore)|
|`template.json`|[dotnet/templating](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Orchestrator.RunnableProjects/Schemas/JSON/template.json)|[SchemaStore/schemastore]( https://github.com/SchemaStore/schemastore/blob/master/src/schemas/json/template.json) - bi-directional|
|`docs` |[dotnet/templating](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/tree/main/docs) | [dotnet/templating/wiki](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/wiki)|

This is a comprehensive action that syncs files from source repo to target repo using pull request. comments.body:
@RehanSaeed thank you for the issue. We'll consider it, however no particular timeline at the moment.

To everyone who is interested in this feature, please let us know in comments that you are interested. Thanks

This would be great to have, but we're still doing planning for the future at this point so we can't say for certain that we'll have the capacity to include it.  We'd love to help any interested community contributors, though.  We have several other PostActionProcessors [here](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/tree/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Cli/PostActionProcessors) that could serve as a basis for any contributions folks would like to add!

More generally, the CLI doesn't have an 'open file in the configured application' Post-Action the way that VS does.  We _can_ and should have one.

A speclet for this would be:

> We provide different handlers for the 'open file' post action on each OS.
>
> On Windows
>  * if powershell is available, invoke the `Invoke-Item` commandlet with the full path to the file: `powershell -Command "Invoke-Item path/to/file"`
>  * if powershell is not available, invoke the `start` builtin of the `cmd.exe` processor: `cmd /c "start path/to/file"`
>
> On MacOS
> * we're running in a user terminal context, so $SHELL points to the current shell program
> * in that shell, run `$SHELL -c "open path/to/file"`
>
> On Linux
> * we're running in a user terminal context, so $SHELL points to the current shell program
> * in that shell, run `$SHELL -c "xdg-open path/to/file"`
> * it's possible that xdg-open doesn't exist (it's part of most distro's dependencies, but no guarantees. should check for this and warn/fail if not present

* [ZTR.Utilities.Templates](https://nuget.org/packages/ZTR.Utilities.Templates)
  * sets the Framework like the dotnet/templating templates do
* [RandomChance.Common.Templates](https://nuget.org/packages/RandomChance.Common.Templates)
  * sets the Framework like the dotnet/templating templates do


All of the external usage feels very copy/pasted from our templates to me. This isn't surprising, given that we don't have a template-for-templates.  I don't think that this functionality is very widely used at the moment.  There is a potential use case for it as a solution to https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3654, however.

No change to this behavior in scope of #2191, the baseline option remains hidden.
Keeping the issue open for discussions.
We should deprecate `baseline` - it's not widely used in the ecosystem and where it is used we have no evidence that template _users_ actually use the baselines.

As it was agreed to deprecate baseline, we need to make all code that uses it obsolete. The action is purely refactoring, until obsolete code is agreed to be removed.

Consider removing `--baseline` option from CLI or make it obsolete.

body:
# .NET Templating as part of broader generative experience

tl;dr; _We have the mechanisms to an experience where users make preliminary decisions on template run, and can then very safely change these experiences as they need. The ways we would alter architectures is the only hard part of the effort, but might align very well with other simplification efforts. A specific use case to consider is authentication._ 

This proposal draws from suggestions and work from Vlada Shubina, David Karlas, Bekir Ozturk, Sayed Hashimi, Phil Henning, Tim Heuer, Brady Gaster and Glenn Condron and others. I think most folks think that this would be a better experience. This paper is heavily opinionated based on my experience with generative practices. 

We have an effective mechanism for most templates today. This is not a replacement for that. This is instead a way to offer a very good user experience for very common templates that we create. Today’s mechanism is based on “runnable templates.” Any changes to templates should retain runnable templates. User actions: 

* Run a template
* Do work
* Make change 
* Do work
* Make change

The next generation of .NET templating can: 

* Retain the commitment to runnable templates
* Be re-entrant and support natural/code based metadata and logical flow based templates (such as T4 or Roslyn source generators) when re-entrant
* Work with, encourage, possibly require special architectures  to isolate code managed by the re-entrant template
* Analyzers and code fixers to support the re-entrant template, where appropriate

This paper describes all those weird words, and then gives an example. 

The approach described here relies on the availability of semantic code analysis (such as the ability to find a reference), and thus is currently applicable to the Roslyn languages – C# and VB.

## What is a “runnable template”?

The concept of “runnable templates” is that the template itself is valid code that can be run in place. This is meaningful only in project templates, because the result of an item template is not runnable by itself. It means that the directory of files the template is built from is a runnable project. This has tremendous value in the ease of creating templates. It also implicitly excludes any (known) logical flow templating mechanism. 

The proposal here is to retain the current templating mechanism. Instead of altering this mechanism, add a follow-on re-entrant mechanism. 

When the user creates the project, template execution would be the current mechanism, and then run a build. The build would run source generators that would also run on future builds. We already do a restore so there will be very little performance hit. Since the source generators also run on future builds, the user merely needs to change their code and generation will run. 

Declarations, anything currently a parameter would become part of the user codes. Examples of what this might look like would be specific class (“new AuthNone(” vs “new AuthAzureMagic(”), method, property and enum usage and/or declaration. 

## What does re-entrant mean in this context?

A re-entrant template is one that you can run again with different metadata and it will alter your code, removing code from the previous run of the template and adding code for the new run. It alters your code in place. See the section Special Architectures. 

It’s also a terrible name. It just happens, the user doesn’t need to deliberately rerun, and it is only a template in the broad sense because it’s a source generator. Its purpose is to apply changes. 

## What is a “logical flow based template”?

Another terrible name I made for the concept of not-runnable and capable of complex analysis. Maybe in this context it should just be called a generator, but I tried to lay this out to encourage alternate thinking – maybe everything is not a generator. Anyway…

Runnable templates have severe limitations. As they exist today, they can’t do loops. Conditionals are via #ifdef so must include blocks of code and are awkward. You can’t build a line of code based on logic so things are simple as the name of a method is impossible. 

A logical flow based template is a template that allows logic, and is not runnable. The common historic example is T4, but there is no reason it can’t be an application. In fact the most important approach to T4 is executable T4 where T4 creates source code that when compiled creates source code. Roslyn source generators are another example of a logical flow based template.

For this project, they aren’t actually a template, they are source generators. Which means, we need no special mechanism to run them. 

_(NOTE: Years ago I mostly wrote a templating language that used additional restrictions on C# to create a templating language. It is not impossible, there are just sufficient limitations a runnable flow based language has to make that it is not practical, and at best requires arcane knowledge. And, at least my approach at the time, required external metadata and successful generative processes today rely on code as metadata. That failure led me to believe that runnable and logical flow templates are exclusive concepts in C# and VB.)_

### Should this effort use T4?

T4 solves a very small part of the problem addressed here. Once you have an architecture (see below) that supports generation, a runnable template to lay out the basic structure and get things ready, a mechanism to rerun the template, and a mechanism to evaluate source code and build the model for generation you’ve done the hard work. Whether the step of generating text is via T4, or interpolated strings, or a set of methods that limit the ways you can mess up the syntax is a small part of the problem. Using T4 will require being able to evaluate a T4 template and that is messy code. The question of T4 both isn’t very important, and we can probably do better for C#/VB code with 2 dozen specialized methods in a library that we can share, and interpolated strings for non C#/VB stuff. 

## What is a “re-entrant template”

It is a generative process that uses the existing code and possibly configuration files to rewrite portions of the code. It requires the ability to find previously generated code to re-write it (destructive generation) and to understand the non-generated code to determine how to re-write.  

This paper is full of bad names. It means it can be run more than once. In this case, there are two templates: A simplified template using the mechanism we know and love today and a reentrant part. In this paper, it is a just a generator that just runs on build.

## What is “natural/code based metadata”

Metadata is the data that drives generation. It is how the user indicates details of the output. Natural metadata is metadata that the user would already create. Examples are databases and source code. Databases are external, in that they are not part of the generated code. User source code is internal metadata in that it is part of the code that is being generated. For example, Auth type and details could be declared in user code. Another example is (a reasonable number of ) parameters passed when `dotnet new` runs

This is in contrast to contrived metadata that exists only for the sake of the generator. Contrived metadata may be necessary when a project is first created. Contrived metadata adds complexity and ideally we would avoid it by requiring no metadata that the user hasn’t entered for another purpose.  

Code based metadata is very important. Roslyn gave us this, although it isn’t easy. Part of the work of this project can be to establish easier ways to understand code from Roslyn (where possible via the code neutral semantic layer, allowing generator guts to be cross language).

## Special architectures

There are many things we can do with templates, but re-entrant templates should only be done with an expectation of altering architectures because safety of reentrancy.

**This is the only hard part of this proposal. Everything else is just work. And these architectures are not radical and will benefit users.**

### Isolation

This section makes the case for the criticality of isolation. If you don’t need to be convinced, skip it.

A principle of code generation is that user code is sacred. It should never be compromised. This is an absolute statement and is approximately impossible to achieve without isolating user code from generated code. If they are together, the user can and will reorder unimportant code, interleave important code of their own and alter the wrapping to suit their tastes. A very sophisticated generator can sort this out (except perhaps the wrapping) _if it knows what the original generated code was_. To know what the original code was requires either maintaining a copy of the code immediately after generation, or knowing all of the metadata (including potentially environmental metadata from another machine if the user receives the code by cloning a repo) and the template for generation. Oh, and you need to have the initial generator as well. Thus, it is very difficult, but possible to do mixed code in Version One of your template. By Version Six, you must also have all previous templates and an indicator of which template was used. Over time mixed output becomes approximately impossible to maintain. Especially when there is an alternative that is also better for the user. 

I have heard _we will recognize whether the user has changed the code and only update the code if they have not_. There are two problems with this statement. The first is that a minor code change like reordering lines should not block future actions, especially since there is no way for the user to know at the time they make the change that they have just hurt their future selves. The second is that it requires you know what template and metadata was used in the initial generation to recognize the code – see earlier discussion on template versioning (or saving the code to a safe location, or saving a hash of the code, all of which is also vulnerable to use deletion). 

I have also heard _we will add a comment warning the user not to change the code_. That has a small problem and a big problem. The small problem is that users do not read comments. The big problem is that unless you put the comment between every line of code the user will never see the comment. The predominate ways we navigate source code do not start at the top.

Isolating generated code is better for the user. Partial classes were introduced for this purpose in .NET in around 2005, and partial classes received an important update alongside Roslyn source generators. One of those updates was that users can’t edit generated files. There is no way to provide this security without separate files.

### Adjusting architectures

Adjusting architectures to embrace re-entrant generation is good for users. We are already doing this very heavily with Roslyn source generators and other changes making ASP.NET architectures much simpler. It is a good time to look at it this in relation to templates. 

A good example is authentication. If we can’t solve auth, then, we failed. Auth has the highest value to users, because asking to do auth when you create your project is silly. They need to do this later once they get things figured out.

### An Example: Auth

Auth has a set of inputs, including what kind of auth and depending on a set of additional information. This information can be placed in a declarative way as part of appropriate code. In the default case this is the only code the user needs to bother with and this is the state after the initial template generation (before the re-entrant generation step). The re-entrant generation runs as source generators in the compile. The user starts their project. 

(This part is vague as it needs ASP.NET input. I would like to sit down with one of the complex templates and walk through what it would look like with this approach and identify challenges.)

There are several kinds of changes the user will make in the lifetime of their project. There are probably files that the user will just change, such as customizing a login page. These may not need to be part of generation, except possibly to offer to remove the file as dead code after an auth change. 

There will also be methods called that the user may want to customize. A default implementation can be generated if, and only if, the user has not provided an implementation (this is how the new partial methods work).

At some point, the user wants to change their authentication. They can either just change it. Any additional information will be obvious and they fix it. Most or all code and information no longer needed just drops or errors. 

One way to implement this would be an AuthInfo base class. Each mechanism for auth would be a derived class with a constructor that with required and optional parameters for all of the information needed for that style of auth. Thus the user would naturally supply the correct information and allow customizations of auth behavior by overriding methods in the specific AuthInfo class. 

With a base/derived class implementation of auth styles, the user changes auth styles by changing the class they are instantiating, and changing therefore changing the constructor that is called. If required information is missing or a parameter is passed that is not valid, the user gets an immediate error and can easily understand why this occurred. 

_Note: This will be much safer if the user elects to used named parameters so Boolean and ints aren’t misunderstood. This is a great case for the future C# feature of properties that are required on initialization, and in that case using initializers instead of constructors. However, that feature doesn’t yet exist so I suggest constructors here._

Analyzers and code fixes can be used to help find dead code that results from changes. This will occur when the user writes a method that is treated as a partial that would normally replace generated code. If the user changes auth so that the method is no longer needed, we may be able to recognize this and remove the unused code. The uncertainty here is only whether the old library would still be present to perform the analysis. If the auth mechanisms are in separate libraries, and the user removes the library before compiling, the dead code may not be flagged. Hmm. Issues to consider.

## And we still need analyzers?

See the section “An example” for an example.

## Isn’t this overly complicated?

Not for users. It optimizes for a great, simple user experience. 

Simple templates are handled well today. This is designed for a known set of problems in Microsoft templates where Roslyn source are in use and the current massively complex templates and lack of ability for users to change their mind is a known problem. Roslyn source generators are a good solution to the problem of reentrancy. The mechanism for generators themselves may be slightly arcane, but is simple. Evaluating code to figure out the code to generate can sometimes be complex. 

## What this does not cover

There are a few classes of problems that this does not handle:

•	Generation based on database metadata: Databases are guaranteed to change, so solutions here need to be re-entrant. I do not think Roslyn source generators have a way to evaluate a database, and it would destroy build performance. But, EF is solving this.
•	Logic during initial template execution.
•	Loads of other stuff I have not thought of.

body:
When a new project is created, can we consider an option to create a new solution as well ? 

I can think of two workflows for new project creation:

(a) Adding a new project to an existing cohort of projects (which may already contain a solution)
(b) Instantiating a brand new cohort of project(s), which could use a solution file for working with IDE. 

I'm interested in improving the experience of the second (b) workflow, which works like this today: 

```pwsh
dotnet new $template
dotnet new sln
dotnet sln add $project
// Use sln
```

I'd like to propose a switch addition to `dotnet new <TEMPLATE>` - `--create-solution | -sln` - which will much like `dotnet new sln`.

The updated `dotnet new` would look like this:

```powershell
dotnet new <TEMPLATE> [--dry-run] [--force] [-lang|--language {"C#"|"F#"|VB}] [-sln|--create-solution]
    [-n|--name <OUTPUT_NAME>] [-o|--output <OUTPUT_DIRECTORY>] [Template options]

dotnet new -h|--help
```

For example, `dotnet new classlib -sln` would generate `classlib.csproj` as well as `classlib.sln`, and `classlib.csproj` to `classllib.sln`. 

Similar to `dotnet new sln`, if a solution file already exists in the location, an error would occur.

comments.body: Can be addressed by https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3208.

This workflow is available today through the [DotnetTemplateMCP](https://github.com/YuliiaKovalova/dotnet-template-mcp) MCP server's `template_compose` tool, which chains multiple template operations in a single orchestrated call.

The exact workflow from this issue (project + solution + sln add) becomes:

```
template_compose(stepsJson=[
  {"templateName": "classlib", "name": "MyLib", "outputPath": "./src/MyLib"},
  {"templateName": "sln", "name": "MyLib", "outputPath": "."}
])
```

This creates the project, creates the solution, and wires them together — equivalent to the proposed `dotnet new classlib -sln`.

For more complex scenarios (API + test project + solution), the same tool scales:

```
template_compose(stepsJson=[
  {"templateName": "webapi", "name": "MyApi", "outputPath": "./src/MyApi"},
  {"templateName": "xunit", "name": "MyApi.Tests", "outputPath": "./tests/MyApi.Tests"},
  {"templateName": "sln", "name": "MyApi", "outputPath": "."}
])
```

See also the related comment on #3208: https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3208#issuecomment-3990754423

Source: [DotnetTemplateMCP](https://github.com/YuliiaKovalova/dotnet-template-mcp) | [NuGet](https://www.nuget.org/packages/DotnetTemplateMCP)

body:
In some cases it is useful to use counters when creating the templates. Example: having the folder for tests with many projects, and next one should increment the previous.

Examples:
```
dotnet new console -o TestConsole??? -> TestConsole001, TestConsole002...
```

Consider what char to use as counter (?,#) etc.

comments.body:
I think you meant to use TestConsole instead of console for the output names: 

```
dotnet new console -o TestConsole??? -> TestConsole001, TestConsole002...
```

and then hopefully if TestConsole002 is the highest number in my folder then `dotnet new console -o TestConsole? -> TestConsole003`. 
And similarly  if TestConsole62 is the highest number in my folder then `dotnet new console -o TestConsole??? -> TestConsole063`.  
if TestConsole1002 is the highest number in my folder then `dotnet new console -o TestConsole1? -> TestConsole003`. 

I would find this useful to have in my toys project folder just to be able to add new project folder easily without looking for the latest number. The 001 gives me the ability to have 999 projects that are ordered correctly in the Explorer, instead of having mstest1, mstest10, mstest 111, mstest2 etc. 

This is how I do it in my powershell profile in mkcd function. it works almost exactly the same as requested here, but I assume you will want to check for ? at the end of the name, and throw error if the dir already exists (and possibly suggest ? there) instead of automatically incrementing. 



```powershell 
function mkcd ($Path) {
    $Path = $ExecutionContext.SessionState.Path.GetUnresolvedProviderPathFromPSPath($Path)
    $name = $Path | Split-Path -Leaf
    $dir = $Path | Split-Path

    mkdir $dir -Force | Out-Null

    $padding = 0
    $prefix = $null

    # if we have ## pattern, make sure we pad the numbers to get 000,
    # and also make sure that any prefix number like 1 are considered so we avoid 
    # creating folder console11 when console1# is provided, console1 already exists
    if ($name -match "^(?<name>.*?)(?<prefix>\d*)(?<padding>#+)$") { 
        # build the number that is the lowest number we should use, and subtract 1
        # so it does not matter if the base number is existing directory or pattern 
        # we will always just increase it by 1 to get the actual final number
        $lowestDesiredNumber = $Matches.prefix + "0"*($Matches.padding.Length) - 1
        # when user requested console### we need to give them 001, not 1
        $padding = $Matches.padding.Length
        $name = $Matches.name
    }
    elseif ($name -match "^(?<name>.*?)(?<prefix>\d+)$") {
        $lowestDesiredNumber = $Matches.prefix - 1
        $padding = 0
        $name = $Matches.name
    }

    $dirs = Get-ChildItem -Directory "$dir/$name*" | Select -ExpandProperty Name | where { $_ -match "^$name\d+$" }

    # check if we found any dirs with numbers at the end, if not just create the dir
    # we could also check for $prefix -eq 0 , and that would create the dir if it did not exist
    # ignoring the existing number dirs e.g. console1 exists, console is requested, 
    # in the current approach we create console2, with checking prefix0 we create console
    if (-not $dirs -and -not (Test-Path $Path)) { 
        mkdir -Path $Path -Force | Out-Null
        cd $Path 
        return
    }
    
    $numbers = @($lowestDesiredNumber) + @( $dirs -replace "^$name(.*)$", '$1' )
    $highest = $numbers | sort { [int]$_ } | Select -Last 1
    $newNumber = [int]$highest+1

    $padding = $highest.Length, $padding | sort -Descending | select -First 1
    $newString = $newNumber.ToString("d$($padding)")

    $new = "$dir\$name$newString"
    mkdir -Force $new | Out-Null
    cd $new
}

gi \t\nums | rmdir -Recurse -Force
mkdir \t\nums -Force | Out-Null
cd \t\nums

mkcd \t\nums\console    # console
mkcd \t\nums\console    # console1
mkcd \t\nums\console    # console2
mkcd \t\nums\console### # console003
mkcd \t\nums\console### # console004
mkcd \t\nums\console### # console005

mkcd \t\nums\mstest1    # mstest1
mkcd \t\nums\mstest1    # mstest2
mkcd \t\nums\mstest##   # mstest03
mkcd \t\nums\mstest1#   # mstest10

mkcd \t\nums\xunit62    # xunit62
mkcd \t\nums\xunit      # xunit63
mkcd \t\nums\xunit####  # xunit0064

ls \t\nums
```

body:
Was thinking, it would enable a lot of ease and usage if the templates can be used without installing it using dotnet new. Can we just use those templates directly from the nugets or a folder to create those items derived from the templates. It may be available now, not sure, but I could not see any available solution for the same.

---

**Audience**: dotnet CLI users

### Background 
Now to instantiate any template you need to install the package containing it first. 
The packages are not updated automatically, and it's user responsibility to keep the up-to-date. To check updates the user needs to use `update` command or will be prompted only after outdated template is created.
In many cases, when acquiring new template, it would be beneficial to try it first to see if it matches your needs.
Now it is a 3 step process:
- install the template package
- instantiate the template
- uninstall the template package

### Justification
- even better experience for CLI users
   - easy option to "try it out" before installing the package
   - avoid running outdated templates - always use latest from the source
- popular tools like npx has this experience

comments.body:
@satyajit-behera is your question about Visual Studio? do you want the templates to be installable in Visual Studio? 

Thank you.

Thanks for the reply. Not really in visual studio. dotnet new works for installed templates. If the templates are directly installed from nuget packages or a folder available in local machine with the same command, it may help a lot in custom template scenarios and multiple version handling.

@satyajit-behera 

do you mean something like this?
`> dotnet new my-template --from MyNuGetPack::1.0.0` - runs `my-template` available in MyNuGetPack nuget.org package (version 1.0.0)
`> dotnet new my-template --from MyFolder` - runs `my-template` from local folder `MyFolder`
Yes. Thanks.

This would be really useful for enabling `npx`-style usage of templates. Project templates especially you often want to use the latest version on each invocation, and a fire-and-forget experience to run the template without having to do the initial install step can really lower the friction to get started.  It also addresses the maintenance aspect of community templates - in the current method you have to update template packages before each invocation if you want to make sure you have the latest. `npx`-style invocation would (effectively) do an install, invoke, cleanup process to ensure that you always have the latest versions.

another idea, originally raised in https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/1680, is to acquire the template on first-time run from known sources (NuGet feeds from nuget.config) if not yet available. Private feeds might be supported using `--add-source` option. 

The challenge is on how to find the template package containing certain template by short name. For NuGet.org, this is already solved as we have search cache containing this information. But this is not available for private feeds. Possible solutions:
- specify package name for this scenario, then the package will be attempted to be installed prior instantiating
- create a way to index private feeds for available templates at user's machine.  The index may be updated once in a while.

I really like this idea. It would make shipping some templates out of band easier, and also easier for people to be on the latest without having to wait for our (Visual Studio) release cycles. npx does have a very good convention for this (essentially, "install and run the thing named this"). I'm not sure if that would play nicely with the difference in template naming and nuget naming conventions in .net and nuget, but we could find some sort of metadata for the nupkg that specifies that templates are there and can be used that way.

> but we could find some sort of metadata for the nupkg that specifies that templates are there and can be used that way

We already have `PackageType` metadata to find templates, and the template metadata itself is in a known location inside such packages - this logic is already what drives the template package indexing that powers `dotnet new search`. So we should have no blockers.

Having this would also let us drop support for several third-party built-in templates, especially in the testing space:

* nunit
* xunit

in favor of letting the actual authors control and express what they want.

The Testing team and the Aspire team have a strong interest in using always-latest templates and would appreciate having this feature.

@thomhurst was requesting TUnit to be available, this feature would allow him to have the same kind of support as other test frameworks providing no-first class (or all first-class) for all our customers

This "npx-style" experience is already available today through the [DotnetTemplateMCP](https://github.com/YuliiaKovalova/dotnet-template-mcp) MCP server (v1.1.0), which wraps the .NET Template Engine for AI-assisted development.

The `template_instantiate` tool does exactly what this issue describes — **auto-resolve from NuGet in a single call**:

1. You call `template_instantiate("some-template", name="MyProject")`
2. If the template isn't installed, it automatically searches NuGet for the best match
3. Installs the package
4. Creates the project

This collapses the 3-step process mentioned in the issue (`install` → `instantiate` → `uninstall`) into one operation. It also resolves latest stable NuGet package versions at creation time, so you never get stale template-hardcoded versions.

### Example

```
template_instantiate("maui", name="MyApp", outputPath="./src/MyApp")
```

If the MAUI template isn't installed, it searches NuGet for the matching package, installs it, then creates the project — all in one call.

The `template_search` tool also provides a unified ranked search across both locally installed templates and NuGet.org, making it easy to discover templates before committing to installation.

While this is an MCP server (designed for AI agents like GitHub Copilot and Claude), the underlying pattern demonstrates that the auto-resolve experience is technically feasible in the template engine itself.

Source: [DotnetTemplateMCP](https://github.com/YuliiaKovalova/dotnet-template-mcp) | [NuGet](https://www.nuget.org/packages/DotnetTemplateMCP)

title: Make dotnet new post actions extendable via components

body:
**Audience**: template authors

### Background 
At the moment a lot of .NET project templates have to manually create similar configuration related to:
- framework
- restore post action
- optional adding of sln 
- language-specific features
- nullable, global usings and other common MSBuild properties
- [AOT configurations](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/31739)
- NuGet Packaging Properties (license, package name, authors, etc)

Moreover more common features will be nice to have:
- optional `editorconfig` (original intention of the issue)
- optional gitignore/gitattributes; git init

Implementing all of above is possible but will result in extra ~300 lines configuration in `template.json` and corresponding testing and maintenance effort. The configuration will be very similar to the same in all the templates.

### Technical suggestion
We are considering to create a specific generator for .NET project templates which implicitly supports the features above. 
All the author needs to do is to opt-in to desired behaviors via corresponding feature flags. 

### Justification
- facilitate much easier entry point for template authoring via simpler configuration
- decrease manual json configuration
- unify configuration for the items above
- unify experience with .NET SDK template

---
original description below
Copying Kathleen's comments from below:

> The template team maintains the .NET standard .editorconfig. Logically this is the same one you get with dotnet new .editorconfig. Templates will not include .editorconfig.
> When the user creates a project, they have the option to use --sln to create the project in a solution (a different feature that this assumes, although it might be later). If this switch is used, a .editorconfig will be placed at the solution level.
> If the user either creates the new project with a parent directory that has a .sln file, or they use the --sln switch, no .editorconfig will be placed in the project file. Otherwise, it will be.
> This might be managed by a post action so template authors could skip it, but we think it is probably the best behavior for all project templates.

The part about -sln is probably not relevant. Therefore, it should be considered out of the scope of this issue.

comments.body: Can you share a bit more details what are you expecting here? Do you expect `dotnet new editorconfig` like https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3195 suggests or you expect `dotnet new console` to include `.editorconfig` file?

Both but my issue is with regards to `dotnet new console` to include .editorconfig file (.NET) template which has the prepopulated default .NET code style, formatting, and naming conventions: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/ide/create-portable-custom-editor-options?view=vs-2019#add-an-editorconfig-file-to-a-project

@mikadumont @jmarolf and I chatted on this. It would be a nightmare to keep all the .editorconfig's consistent if we put them into every template, and then it would be a bad experience for users to wind up with multiple editor config's  (per project) instead of one (per repo). That said, we love .editorconfig and want it in every repo :-) Thus, a new more complex feature!

A rough outline: 

* The template team maintains _the_ .NET standard .editorconfig. Logically this is the same one you get with `dotnet new .editorconfig`. Templates will _not_ include .editorconfig.
* When the user creates a project, they have the option to use --sln to create the project in a solution (a different feature that this  assumes, although it might be later). If this switch is used, a .editorconfig will be placed at the solution level.
* If the user either creates the new project with a parent directory that has a .sln file, or they use the --sln switch, no .editorconfig will be placed in the project file. Otherwise, it will be. 
* This might be managed by a post action so template authors could skip it, but we think it is probably the best behavior for all project templates.

This sounds like another scenario where something like `dotnet
 new repo` would be useful…
The details of the design can be found [here](https://microsoft-my.sharepoint.com/:w:/p/kdollard/ESAbYFLrDoRPhvMhMI0kO4IB0I1DMS3ki7rY7nBgnCYCqA) (internal).

Hi - this multi-template workflow is something I've solved in [dotnet-template-mcp](https://github.com/YuliiaKovalova/dotnet-template-mcp), an MCP server that wraps the .NET Template Engine for AI-assisted scaffolding.

The `template_compose` tool chains multiple template operations in a single call:

```json
[
  {"templateName": "webapi", "name": "MyApi", "outputPath": "./src", "parametersJson": "{\"auth\": \"Individual\"}"},
  {"templateName": "sln", "name": "MyApi"},
  {"templateName": "gitignore", "target": "."}
]
```

This creates the project, the solution file, and the .gitignore in one step — exactly the `dotnet new <TEMPLATE> --sln` workflow requested here. The server also auto-adds the project to the solution.

Additionally, `solution_analyze` inspects existing `.sln` files to understand the workspace context before creation, so the agent can make informed decisions about where to place new projects.

It doesn't replace a native CLI flag, but for AI-assisted development workflows it solves the same pain point today. Available as: `dotnet tool install -g DotnetTemplateMCP`.

body:
**Audience**: authors (advanced)

### Background
Allow custom extensibility scenarios for the templates.

The template engine already considers extensibility by using components. Component is a class implementing [`IIdentifiedComponent`](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Abstractions/IIdentifiedComponent.cs) interface. Template engine is managing components in [`ComponentManager`](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Edge/Settings/ComponentManager.cs) class.
At the moment the only way to install additional components is from code (adding components via `ITemplateEngineHost` or adding components via `IEngineEnvironmentSettings.ComponentManager`. 
To allow extensibility scenario:
- the way of adding and managing additional assemblies with components should be implemented. The initial (currently disabled) implementation is available in [`Scanner.ScanForComponents`](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/301a5747cb4f317b49a32a2b5a652250e2220f33/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Edge/Settings/Scanner.cs#L137) method. Detected components are not saved to settings.
- installing additional assemblies should be surfaced via command available in `dotnet new`.

Already defined components suitable for extensibility for template authoring:
- generators ([`IGenerator`](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Abstractions/IGenerator.cs))
- macros (generated symbols) in runnable projects generator ([`IMacro`](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Orchestrator.RunnableProjects/Abstractions/IMacro.cs) and its derived classes)
- constraints ([`ITemplateConstraintFactory`](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Abstractions/Constraints/ITemplateConstraintFactory.cs))
- post actions ([`IPostActionProcessor`](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/main/src/Cli/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Cli/PostActionProcessors/IPostActionProcessor.cs)

Missing parts:
- acquisition/distribution workflow for components assemblies/packages
- managing the component assemblies versions (different templates may require the same component of different version)
- documentation

### Justification
- give advanced authors more customization beyond standard features of template engine

Related issues:
- [x] [Components issues #2727](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/2727)
- [ ] Move `IPostActionProcessor` component to Abstractions https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3225
- [x] https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/2723

comments.body:
@mikeyoshino 
Unfortunately, at the moment there is no way to force the template output be created to directory when `-n` or `-o` is not specified.

As a workaround, you can put the template content to subfolder ('GeneratedCode') inside the template definition and set `preferNameDirectory` to false. To allow the user change the name of that subfolder, you can use parameter symbol (`--folder-name`, as example) that renames the default subfolder name. However to do that user should use `--folder-name`, and not `-n`.

I will keep the issue open so we can discuss proper solution for this case.

body:
As a template author, I want a way to validate the templates, so that I can validate template before the publish.
**Audience**: template authors

## Background
The template configuration requires manual editing in of JSON configuration which is source of authoring mistakes.
The configuration involves a lot of conditions, which are not validated in any way until the template is being generated.
When grouping the templates the configuration is manually, and requires careful combination of the fields across multiple JSON files. The grouping errors are shown only when the template is being run (not when the package containing it is installed)

## Planned validation checks:

(note: though some of the issues are closed, their comments contain suggested validation check)

- Blacklist top level commands from allowed template names/shortnames
- Flag optional parameters without default value
- Flag parameters that are prefixes of others (this can create ambiguous situations when parsing expressions via tries)
- All forms applied to source name provide different results (warning, see https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/1920)
- All forms applied to symbol provide different results
- https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3828
- https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/4268
- https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/5561 (nth)
- https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3254
- https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3127
- https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/5198
- https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/5671 - the template doesn't define `name` parameter/symbol
- https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/4650

## Justification
- decrease the number of issues when authoring 1st party templates and detecting them post PR/even releasing them 
- improve easiness of authoring and quality of 3rd party templates; detect potential issues prior to testing
- improve UX for final users by not allowing to install invalid templates / warning about possible issues 

## Technical details
We plan to expose 2 ways:
- via MSBuild tasks, see: https://github.com/dotnet/templating/issues/3828
- via authoring tools CLI 
Both MSBuild task and CLI tool already exist.

As part of this task, the validation in template engine and `dotnet new` should be improved as well.
- when reading the template, the generator should ensure it has a minimum required set of information in order to proceed. The JSON parsing errors and basic errors and warnings should be exposed.
- when installing the template, the conflicts should be detected
- the host should be able to inject the checks for `host.json` file.
- the way to present the errors should be potentially implemented in host itself

Feedback from @sayedihashimi 
- Templates shouldn’t have to be installed in order to be validated
    - More specifically be able to pass in a folder path or a path to .nupkg file
- The tool should accept multiple values for folder path/path to .nupkg
    - For authors that have developed several templates this would be helpful
- After running the tool it should return a non-zero exit code if the validation is not successful
    -  This will enable users to script the validate step, and be able to fail the CI build if so
- Error and warning messages should follow the MSBuild error/warning format so that errors/warnings should be auto-detected if a user executes the tool via an MSBuild file.
    -  The MSBuild team may know of any formal docs.
    - [MSBuild book](https://nam06.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Famzn.to%2F3mMBLUY&data=04%7C01%7Cvshubina%40microsoft.com%7Ccda6a1eb1a0d4738abbe08d87f750ca7%7C72f988bf86f141af91ab2d7cd011db47%7C1%7C0%7C637399488001326850%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C1000&sdata=PDWlvfCi4ORE%2B%2Bv8E5ifmJQHPn2TZawmbEHPwmmgpYU%3D&reserved=0)

comments.body: How does this fit in with @sayedihashimi 's tool?
One of the things we should validate for is the use of parens around complex conditions as discussed in #2209

> How does this fit in with @sayedihashimi 's tool?

I think the idea is to have some similar validation, but it's built into `dotnet new` instead of a stand alone tool.

> The tool should accept multiple values for folder path/path to .nupkg

This is good, but in addition to this I think that when a folder path is specified, the tool should search the folder recursively for all templates. If a user is authoring a template pack (i.e. AWS/Uno/etc) they can pass the root folder to the validator and then it will discover all the templates that the folder contains.
I am cool with your thought process, @KathleenDollard .  Seems worth the story points vs the other discussion.

The following was already done:
- https://github.com/dotnet/templating/pull/5838 - validation infrastructure was implemented. Validation checks can be inserted via components (`ITemplateValidator` and `ITemplateValidatorFactory` implementations). Existing checks were reimplemented in this infrastructure. `ITemplateValidator` and `ITemplateValidatorFactory` are currently internal but ready to be made public once the feature is fully ready for release.
- https://github.com/dotnet/templating/pull/5839 - validation was added to authoring tools CLI (via `validate` command) with no additional checks at the moment. It is possible to add additional checks by implementing `ITemplateValidator` and `ITemplateValidatorFactory` interfaces, adding them as additional component when loading host.
- https://github.com/dotnet/templating/pull/5840 - validation was added as MSBuild task (`Validate`) with no additional checks at the moment.

The following tasks remain:
- implementing additional validation checks (see planned checks list in issue description)
- making interfaces public to allow extensibility by tools/hosts
- implementing checks in hosts, in particular for `host.json` configuration
- updating documentation and authoring tools guidelines.

I've implemented several of the validation checks listed in this issue as part of the [DotnetTemplateMCP](https://github.com/YuliiaKovalova/dotnet-template-mcp) MCP server (v1.1.0). The `template_validate` tool performs offline validation of `template.json` files — no template installation required, just point it at a file path.

### Checks implemented from this issue's list:

| Planned check | Status |
|---------------|--------|
| Blacklist top-level commands from allowed shortNames | ✅ Flags conflicts with `build`, `run`, `test`, `publish`, `pack`, `restore`, `new`, `clean`, `sln` |
| Flag optional parameters without default value | ✅ Warns on choice/bool parameters missing `defaultValue` |
| Flag parameters that are prefixes of others | ✅ Detects prefix collisions (e.g., `auth` vs `authMode`) |
| Validate JSON parsing / required fields | ✅ Checks `identity`, `name`, `shortName` presence and format |
| Templates shouldn't have to be installed to validate | ✅ Parses `template.json` directly via `System.Text.Json` |

### Additional checks beyond the original list:

- Parameter datatype validation (`bool`, `string`, `int`, `float`, `hex`, `text`, `choice`)
- Choice parameter completeness (choices defined, default matches a valid choice)
- Computed/generated symbol completeness (e.g., `replaces` without `value`)
- Post-action configuration gaps
- Constraint validation (missing/invalid rules)
- Tag recommendations (missing `language`, `type` tags)

### How to use it:

The tool is available through the MCP server and can be called by any MCP-compatible AI assistant:

```
template_validate(templateJsonPath="path/to/.template.config/template.json")
→ { valid: true/false, errors: [...], warnings: [...], suggestions: [...] }
```

It returns structured JSON with categorized issues — errors (must fix), warnings (should fix), and suggestions (nice to have).

This doesn't cover the MSBuild task integration or the CLI authoring tool aspects of the issue, but it provides an AI-accessible validation path that covers most of the JSON-level checks. The non-zero exit code requirement is naturally handled since the MCP tool returns structured error data that the calling agent can act on.

Source: [template_validate implementation](https://github.com/YuliiaKovalova/dotnet-template-mcp/blob/main/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.MCP/Tools/TemplateValidateTool.cs) | [PR #17](https://github.com/YuliiaKovalova/dotnet-template-mcp/pull/17)

body:
**Problem:**
- Template release cycle involves manual actions at the moment that are likely to be not needed.
- Template packages seems to use 2 different versioning approaches:
  - release separate package for each TFM in all the versions (dotnet/templating templates, aspnet)
  - release one package/one template supporting all TFMs in the version (wpf, winforms, test)
which makes release and distribution workflow different. 
- Template packages are published to NuGet.org frequently without any change except version bump. The version publishing is non-linear, as older TFM packages are also shipped with the servicing: example: 3.1 is shipped 3 times as of now: with 3.1 servicing, with 5.0 servicing and 6.0 preview.

The following points should be addressed:
- the release and versioning approached should be unified between repos
- consider creating separate repo for all templates under common structure and versioning
- clarify versions to be inserted to installer branches: does it need previous versions to be included? 
  - if not guidance on needed manual steps on branding should be changed, and non-needed entries should be removed from props file in dotnet/installer (unify across all the template packages)
- clarify which packages should be shipped to Nuget.org and their versions (unify across all the template packages)
- clarify if we should do shipping the package in case of no change to template content (unify across all the template packages)
- consider changing location of templates when installed from C:\Program Files\dotnet\templates\<runtimeVersion> to C:\Program Files\dotnet\sdk\<sdkVersion>\templates

body:
Is there a way to perform mathematical operations on a parameter or generate some sequential values?

My use case is pretty simple, but I imagine the solution could be applied to a multitude of use cases. I'm building a template for my team to use for generating a series of applications and we have a need for each application to be generated with a different PORT assigned to each. 

For example, when we generate a new web API project using the built-in template, in launchSettings.json it automatically assigns port 5000 to HTTP, and 5001 to HTTPS.

I'm currently using the 'port' generator to assign a random available port to the HTTP protocol. I would like to have the HTTPS port continue to be HTTP port + 1 but have not found a way to do so yet.  Is there any way to do this?

comments.body:
It is impossible to perform arithmetic operations on a parameter, unfortunately. 
I am putting this issue in the Low Pri Backlog, as we also have no plans to implement this feature in the nearest future.

BTW, it seems that it is [possible](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/12941362/is-it-possible-to-increment-numbers-using-regex-substitution) to increment integers using regular expressions, you may try to use this to achieve your goal.

I second the suggestion/request/issue.

What if the "evaluate" or "computed" generators were able to perform simple arithmetics?

Maybe they already can. However, the examples I've seen so far are only using boolean expressions.

For example I tried:
```json
"serviceHttpPort": {
   "type": "generated",
   "generator": "port",
   "parameters": {
      "low": 1024,
      "high": 6000,
      "fallback": 1433
   },
   "replaces": "7511"
},
"serviceHttpsPort": {
   "type": "computed",
   "datatype": "int",
   "value": "serviceHttpPort + 1",
   "replaces": "7512"
},
```
This didn't work though (yet?).

We're also interested in a feature like this for the in-box ASP.NET Core templates. In .NET 6 we're changing the default server profile to Kestrel (from IIS Express) and as such we're [updating the templates](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/34363) to utilize the existing port generation feature.

Kestrel defaults to HTTP port 5000 and HTTPS port 5001 if none are specified, and most apps are configured to auto-redirect from HTTP:5000 to HTTPS:5001, so we'd really like for the HTTP port to default to the lower end of the supplied range, rather that the [random start it does today](https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/94b1e0839ab49026b3ff654f2b5e5e1a1b4b2c53/src/Microsoft.TemplateEngine.Orchestrator.RunnableProjects/Macros/Config/GeneratePortNumberConfig.cs#L32). It would also be really nice if the two ranges (HTTP, HTTPS) could be paired in the same generator to attempt to produce some symmetry, e.g. if the HTTP port range is 5000-5300 and the HTTPS range is 7000-7300, attempt to use them in pairs, e.g. 5000/7000, 5001/7001, etc.

That way, HTTP ports for newly created ASP.NET Core apps will generally be 5000 (the same as running from the CLI today) and the HTTPS port will be 7000 (nice symmetry and usually will be redirected to automatically by the app),  **unless** there is another app running on port 5000 or 7000 already, in which case it would be 5001 and 7001, and so on.

Thanks @CodyDunlap. The only issue with that is it doesn't check that the httpsPort isn't currently in use. To do this "properly" it would need to be logic in the generator to ensure both ports aren't in use at the time the project is created. Super neat though!

We don't plan to do it now, but our project is open to contributing this feature.
You can find some details here: https://github.com/dotnet/templating/blob/main/docs/contributing/how-to-create-new-generated-symbol.md
